abstract_cert: On the public CMU CERT r4.2 insider-threat benchmark (1,000 users, 70 insiders), on which the system was not designed, the out-of-the-box detector found only 3 of 36 held-out insiders, showing that its behavioural layers ignore the small deviations of quiet insiders. Adding one generic indicator, removable-media use by an account with no such history, raised this to 22 of 36 at under one alert per day, including every insider of the first scenario, while gradual data theft by job-seeking insiders remained largely undetected.
dataset_cert: the standard public benchmark: 1,000 simulated employees over 17 months (January 2010 to May 2011) with 70 malicious insiders in three scenarios. The full data set (about 16 GB) was converted with the project's adapter into 12.8 million events and analysed in full (Section 10.5).
exp_cert: the full data set (1,000 users, 70 insiders) analysed with January to May 2010, before any malicious activity, as the learning period. The system was run exactly as designed on the simulated organisation (out-of-the-box) and again with one generic insider indicator added afterwards (rule R16). To keep that addition honest, the users were split at random into a development half and a held-out test half, each with half of the insiders; R16 was chosen on the development half only, and the test half is what is reported.
timing_cert: the CERT analysis (12.8 million events, about 2,000 users and computers over 17 months) takes about 8 minutes with a peak memory use of 6.4 GB.
cert_intro: Table 10.6 reports the results on the held-out half of the CERT r4.2 users (113,374 user-days in the detection window, June 2010 to May 2011, of which 475 are malicious). The answer key labels 72 accounts: the 70 insiders and two supervisors whose accounts were misused by scenario-3 insiders. An insider counts as detected if an alert was raised on at least one of their malicious days.

cert_layers_intro: Table 10.7 and Figure 10.4 show why the out-of-the-box result is weak: on CERT the statistical and machine-learning layers rank user-days barely better than chance, and almost all of the ranking comes from the rules.
cert_discussion: The cause is calibration. The behavioural layers were designed on the simulated organisation, whose attacks are loud (gigabytes uploaded, dozens of failed logins), and they deliberately ignore deviations below three robust standard deviations and machine-learning scores below the 99th percentile of normal days; this is what keeps false alarms to about one a day. CERT insiders are quiet: a first USB connection, a few visits to job sites, a handful of after-hours logons. These fall inside the band the system was built to ignore, so on most malicious days the behavioural layers contribute nothing and the fused score rests on the rules; the weak job-site rule alone gives most scenario-2 days a risk of only 10.

The out-of-the-box result was frozen and is reported as the generalisation result. One generic insider-threat indicator was then added: removable-media use by an account that never used removable media in its learning period (rule R16, MITRE ATT&CK T1052.001, weight 0.45 like the comparable exfiltration rules). It is not specific to CERT, where 77% of users never use removable media, as in many organisations that restrict USB storage; it never fires on the simulated organisation, whose results are unchanged; and it was chosen on the development half, where it raised the insiders detected from 4 to 17 of 36. On the untouched test half it raised them from 3 to 22 of 36, while alerts rose only from 0.66 to 0.84 a day for about 500 users. It catches every scenario-1 insider and three of the four scenario-3 insiders, but not the job seekers of scenario 2, who already used USB drives and simply used them more; catching them needs behavioural layers that respond to smaller deviations.

For an analyst who reviews the three riskiest users each day (0.3% of users), 28 of the 36 held-out insiders appear on the list on at least one malicious day (Figure 10.4b). Day-level precision stays low (0.15) because the long scenario-2 windows contribute most malicious days. The results are not directly comparable with the models in Chapter 2, which use labelled training data or per-session sequences; this system uses no labels and daily aggregates.
discussion_extra: The CERT benchmark makes the main limitation concrete. On data it was not designed on, the system's behavioural layers were too conservative: out of the box only 3 of 36 held-out insiders were detected. One generic indicator raised this to 22 of 36 at under one alert a day, but insiders whose behaviour changes only by degree (scenario 2) remain hard. Precision on the simulated organisation (0.964) should therefore be read as an upper bound, and the threshold, weights and calibration as settings to tune per organisation.
conclusion_cert: On the independent CERT r4.2 benchmark the out-of-the-box system detected only 3 of 36 held-out insiders, because its behavioural layers were calibrated to ignore small deviations; with one generic insider indicator it detected 22 of 36, including every scenario-1 insider, at under one alert a day, while gradual data theft by job-seeking insiders remained largely undetected.
future_eval: make the behavioural layers respond to many small deviations (continuous scores calibrated per organisation) so that gradual insiders such as CERT scenario 2 are caught, and evaluate on CERT r5.2 / r6.2 and the real CLUE-LDS logs [3].
